Portions of the document, prepared in Arabic by the Iraqi government, was translated and broadcast by ABC News on September 11, and were the basis of accounts by The Washington Post and The Guardian of London. TTie article states:
The State Department declined to confirm the accuracy of the document, but officials did not dispute Ms Glaspie's essential message.
Then it states:
The administration was following what President Bush acknowledged last week was a flawed policy toward Iraq, a policy built on the premise that the best way to handle Mr. Hussein and moderate his behaviour was through improving relations with Baghdad. That assessment presumed that Iran and Iraq, both exhausted by their eight-year border war, would focus on domestic reconstruction, not foreign adventurism.
As a result, the Bush Administration failed to calibrate its policy to take into account a string of belligerent statements and actions by Mr. Hussein in recent months, including the execution of a British journalist and a threat to use chemical weapons against Israel.
Listen to this, Mr. Speaker:
"We were essentially operating without a policy," said a senior administration official. "The crisis came in a bit of a vacuum, at a time when everyone was focusing on German reunification."
This lady we have seen on PBS over the year because she speaks for the administration quite a bit:
On July the 24, when Margaret D. TUtwiler, the States Department spokeswomen, was asked whether the United States had any commitment to defend Kuwait,she said"We do not have any defence

November 28, 1990

treaties with Kuwait, and there are no special defense or security commitments to Kuwait."
Asked whether the United States would help Kuwait if it were attacked, she replied, "We also remain strongly committed to supporting the individual and collective self-defense of our friends in the gulf with whom we have deep and longstanding ties," a statement that some Kuwaiti officials said privately was too weak.
Tivo days before the invasion, John H. Kelly, Assistant Secretaiy of State for Near Eastern and South Asian Affairs, essentially repeated the same message in Congressional testimony.
Lee Hamilton, at the hearing, chided Mr. Kelly for not taking a tougher stance against Iraq in his testimony before the invasion. The article goes on:
You left the impression that it was the policy of the United States not to come to the defense of Kuwait," said Mr. Hamilton, an Indiana Democrat. "I asked you if there was a U.S. commitment to come to Kuwait's defense if it was attacked. Your response over and over again was we have no defense-treaty relationship with any gulf country."
I will not go any further because others wish to speak. Time is very essential in any types of conclusion. In conclusion, we had this type of flip-flop in policy when mixed signals were sent to the president by the ambassador for the United States. Fortunately, Bush did stabilize those mixed signals, but we may get ourselves involved in a world war. If there is any doubt about fighting, everyone in this House and everyone at the United Nations should read the book The Bodyguard of Lies. In it Churchill is quoted as saying: "In war truth is so precious it must be protected by a bodyguard of lies".
I commend this to everybody to read because this is the story of the deception, the deceit, and the spies, not just during the war but before the war when the German Commander in Chief, General Beck, of the German general staff was trying to get a message to London in 1938, saying: "Hey, London, we will get rid of this madman Hitler if you make sure you don't do certain things". This story illustrates in quote after quote and person after person how even within the general staff, the head of the intelligence department of the German army was always trying to get messages through.
If these two cultures that think alike could not get the message through to prevent a war, how can we be expected to hurry the type of communication that
Government Orders
obviously is a problem between an Arabic situation and our western situation?
I conclude with what a Christian told me at a New Year's levee during the Iran hostage situation when poor old President Carter was trying to get the hostages out. I will never forget this. This was told by a member of our Armed Forces at the base that I have the honour to represent, CFB Greenwood. He is a Christian now. He had been a Muslim. He told me: "Mr. Nowlan, what really is the trouble with you westerners trying to deal with us people in the Middle East, you do not understand us because fundamentally the quickest way a Muslim can get to heaven is to kill an infidel and every Christian is an infidel. If you cannot get to heaven that way, the second quickest way to get to heaven is to be killed by an infidel".
With that type of so different thinking, to think that we are hurrying this thing along and not giving the time that most experts say is necessary for trade sanctions, I say we will regret it. This debate has been important. I only hope it gets to some people in New York before tomorrow.

Mr. Speaker, it was an interesting, very worth-while and entertaining presentation.
There are two interesting things that I would like to ask the member about the speech. One, he is a longstanding Conservative and respected member of the Conservative Party and the government in this House who recently crossed the floor. In his statement tonight he opposes the motion. He pointed out the difficulties in the vagueness of that resolution and the fact that the opposition could interpret it the way they have tonight. The other thing is the consistency of the government side of the House where they are rock solid for this resolution and speak in support of it.
Would the hon. member venture to guess that the reason that they are on side is the government caucus is being forced into this position and the fact that the member has crossed the floor has given him the freedom to speak out against a very poor resolution presented to this House?

Categorically no, Mr. Speaker, I would not subscribe to that at all. Some day if the hon. member's party ever gets to be the government he will

November 28, 1990
Government Orders
understand that there are some different pressures, but he can still speak out, he can still speak within and then he can make up his mind. I think the debate here tonight typified that. Things were said by members on all sides that frankly were not strictly according to the dots on the i's and the crosses on the t's of the party lines.
I would like to see, frankly, more independence sometimes in the hon. member's party because his party is more monolithic than any party that I ever belonged to.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was delighted to hear the feast of reason and flow of soul from the hon. member. It is wonderful that, having switched sides, he is able to become unzipped as it were and spill out all these wonderful thoughts for the benefit of all members of this House and, of course, for the Canadian public. What I want to ask him and what I could not understand from listening as attentively as I did to his lengthy speech was whether or not he is going to support the Liberal amendment to this motion.

Mr. Speaker, I have great respect for the member for Niagara, even when I was sitting on the other side of the House, although he used to confound me sometimes with his semantic arguments on procedural hurdles that had no sense, but you did not hear-

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: I'm from Kingston.

Kingston, sorry. Well, you sometimes sound like Niagara on your procedural points of privilege. That is what I thought.
I am sorry the member did not hear me too clearly because I thought I did say at one time when I was trying to speak a little slower than I usually speak that I was going to support your amendment.

Mr. Speaker, just a quick question. The member has been in the House for a considerable period of time. Perhaps he can shed some light on the NDP amendment.
The NDP amendment says that this House opposes the use of force against Iraq until sanctions and other UN measures have had time to succeed. In effect what the NDP is saying is that they are endorsing the use of force, which seems to be contrary to NDP policy. Perhaps the member, with his experience, can advise the House whether this is an about-face on behalf of the
NDP who seem to be supporting war with this particular amendment. Does he share my conclusions?

I will be even shorter on this one.
Just because I moved across the floor of the House to this perch that has a great view is no sign that I am going to start to interpret NDP amendments, subamendments, or even motions. I think they are quite capable of trying to interpret themselves.
[Translation)

I have a short question, Mr. Speaker. I am aware of my colleague's experience and I would like him to tell me, based on his many years in the House-during his career, he has taken part in debates which were just as important as this one-in view of the circumstances and of the importance of the issue and considering that motion No. 24 which we are studying this evening is meant to support action to be taken by the United Nations, whether he would agree with me that the members of this House should all stand behind Canada's support of the United Nations.

This has been part of the debate, Mr. Speaker, and I appreciate and know that the member has dutifully been here tonight and has had good questions. This is part of the debate. Obviously we all want to support the UN, but there is obviously a little different interpretation as how you most effectively support it, especially when you have a resolution that I think even my hon. friend would agree has some vagueness to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate, the hon. member for Fredericton-York-Sunbury and the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte will be the next two speakers with 10 minutes each.

Mr. Speaker, this is a debate which I think we all wish was not necessaiy. Certainly it is one I would have preferred to avoid, but I feel it is a personal political responsibility to take a stand on difficult issues like this, perhaps particularly so on difficult issues like this.
It is unthinkable that we have come to this tonight. I do not think many of us ever believed we would again have to come to grips with the real prospects of war. It is a little like a nightmare, unreal, unimaginable that we must seriously consider decisions that will bear potential for death and destruction, not only of Canadian men and women, but possibly of tens of thousands of human
November 28. 1990

beings on all sides, friends and foes, not just military personnel but innocent civilians, families, and children. It certainly is a horrible prospect.
My own instincts, as I believe would be the case with virtually every member in this Elouse, would normally be to work for peace at almost any cost. Certainly I believe that we should do that. We should work for peace at almost any cost. Certainly I know that most of my constituents would have us avoid armed conflict except as a very last resort.
It is not difficult for me to identify with this issue in a very personal way. My wife and I have raised seven children and we have seven grandchildren. It is not inconceivable that war in the Persian Gulf might eventually impact directly on their lives. The world is a very small place today and distances are covered quickly by satellites, aircraft, intercontinental missiles, and, yes indeed, even by nuclear bombs.
It is very tempting, and it would be with great relief to set this subject aside, to leave it to other countries with larger stakes in the issues and with larger capabilities to deal with them. It would be far more satisfying to speak only for peace and never in contemplation of war.
That would not be responsible in the context of our membership in the United Nations. It would not be true to our commitments of interdependence with our allies, our neighbours and our friends. It would not be respectful of the faith in our mandates from our constituents, and I do not believe it would be Canada.
Rather, we have no alternative but to face up to the tragic irony that, although peace is the goal we all seek, history has taught us that sometimes if we want to ensure peace, we must even be prepared to go to war to attain it. This truly does seem to be one of those times in world history.
Not necessarily war, but a resolve for war if necessary to preserve the peace. I believe it is that resolve that will be our strength in preventing war at this time in the Persian Gulf.
I have always thanked my maker that I was born too young to fight in Europe or in Japan, but I do remember. Looking back those more than 50 years, I think we can
Government Orders
now see with the perfect vision of hindsight that appeasement of dictators does not work to ensure peace.
Perhaps if Hitler had been confronted strongly and with determination in the late 1930s, the world might have been saved from the destruction of World War II, and many millions of lives might not have been lost.
Similarly, in 1990, I think the analogy does bear consideration that if the territorial ambition of Iraq, smaller than Germany but no less aggressive, and its dictator, Saddam Hussein, less powerful than Hitler but made from the same mould, and if their blatant aggression is not stopped in its tracks now, then who can tell where it may lead?
Our quest for peace and security cannot long tolerate the risks that that unanswered question contains. Will it stop at Kuwait? Will it be contained in the Middle East? Will it involve nuclear weapons? Can we really tolerate any of those questions at risk?
As compelling as those questions are, the burden of this debate does bear heavily upon us all. It was put in context for me today by an aggressive TV reporter on my way into the House when he asked: "Mr. Bird, are you really going to vote for young Canadians to come home in body bags from the Persian Gulf? Are you really going to obey orders from the U.S.A.?"
My quick answer seemed somehow inept and inadequate, almost as though these cynical and tortuous barbs were beyond my competence to answer. Yet, as I reflected upon these issues throughout the day, I believe I had them right at the start. I said to him: "I am not voting for death in the Persian Gulf, but rather I am voting for the best prospects of life and peace for this and future generations. I am not voting for the U.S.A. or any other foreign initiative, but rather for Canada to fulfil its responsibilities as a founding member of the United Nations designed so long ago as our best hope for preserving world peace".
Perhaps I could have even said more. For example, a little more than two weeks ago, we observed Remembrance Day in Canada. We paid tribute to hundreds of thousands of Canadians who fought for this country in two World Wars and in Korea, a great many of whom gave their lives in pursuit of freedom and peace.

Government Orders
It has long been part of our commitment on Remembrance Day to make the commitment that their sacrifices shall not have been in vain. We have not only a responsibility today to present and future generations, but also an obligation to the memory of our forebears: our fathers, brothers and uncles that we shall do what it takes to preserve peace in the world and indeed, yes, in many cases to our sisters, our aunts and our mothers.
It is a tragic statement, but to keep this commitment we must contemplate today the prospect of war again. That is a position I feel sure that those past generations, and indeed future generations, will understand and respect.
Our first challenge is to demonstrate our resolve and our diplomatic skills to mount deterrent influence that will pre-empt the prospects of conflict. The economic blockade against Iraq is a powerful weapon. It must be used with ever-increasing discipline and intensity.
In the final analysis, however, we must make it terribly obvious that we are prepared to join the United Nations in whatever fight it takes to turn Iraq out of Kuwait and to stop its aggression completely. It is to be hoped, indeed it is to be prayed, that such a demonstration of economic sanctions and political will be sufficient to achieve the purposes of peace. Otherwise the cause of peace may demand the action of war and ultimately, with very heavy hearts yet resolute spirits, we may be called upon and we must be prepared to help fight it.
The entire area of the Middle East is now a flash point for world conflict. There are many volatile forces at work, none of which can be totally predictable, except that their impact will have profound consequences around the globe. Never, since its inception, has the United Nations represented such potential for world action toward peace, and never before has its mission led so closely to war.
Perhaps, to use a Churchillian phrase, this may become the United Nations' finest hour, when the consensus and strength of nations united for peace can demonstrate conclusively that they are capable of preserving it, even by force, if necessary to do so. There can be no compromise of the principles of respect for
sovereignty of other nations and defence against aggression over the weak by the strong.
Let us hope and pray that in demonstrating its commitment to those principles, in the face of Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, the United Nations will also be delivering an unmistakable message of resolve that will help bring resolution to other Middle East conflicts as well. Ultimately, the fires of war must be banked in all comers of the world, particularly in the Middle East. Preserving peace in the Persian Gulf may prove to be the prelude to permanent peace elsewhere throughout that troubled region, and indeed throughout the world.

Mr. Speaker, we have heard from both sides tonight differing versions of what is going on in the world and what is going on in the Persian Gulf. I think we have to respect both sides. If Canadian people who are watching tonight can filter this debate to its lowest common denominator, I guess they will come up with the understanding that we are trying to say tonight is that we do want peace. Everyone in this House wants peace.
I can criticize the New Democrats for their position. I can criticize the Liberals for their position, and maybe some of our own Progressive Conservatives. However, if one were to cut through all the rhetoric and political posturing on both sides of the House, I think one would find that the common denominator is peace, to maintain peace in the Middle East.
If the Canadian people have had a chance to hear our Associate Minister of National Defence and our Minister of National Defence who is in the House at this very moment, they will come to the opinion that that is what they want. There is absolutely no question about it.
When we compare what is going on in the Persian Gulf at this very moment to what has gone on in Vietnam and in Europe during World War II under the dictates of Adolf Hitler, I do not think it is a fair comparison. I think some members draw those comparisons simply out of fear, because we do not want those types of things to happen. If we measure what has happened in this so-called civilized world of ours in the last hundred years, in fact within the last 20th century starting with World War II and going through, there is no question at all that war is the most inhumane of all activities that human beings engage in. We do not want it. Millions of lives have been lost forever. Young generations of Canadians did not have an opportunity to grow up and
November 28, 1990

experience the great country that we do have. It was the same for Allied Forces in European countries and the United States of America.
We can go through all of the wars that we have been engaged in as a peacekeeping nation. None of us will question the fact that Canada is a peacekeeping nation, yet at some particular point we have had to put our men, our women, our children, our country on the line. Other nations have done the same thing in defence of certain principles. We have paid the price, not as much as other countries but we have certainly paid the price: hundreds of thousands of Canadians, millions of Europeans, countless millions of Russians. War has devastated the world in terms of human tragedy. None of us want to see that.
That is exactly what we are attempting to do in the Middle East. We have the support of just about eveiy civilized nation in the world in what we are attempting to do as a nation: maintain the peace. We do not want to see the kind of devastation brought about by war, but we do not avoid war by backing down and allowing an aggressive nation to take advantage of a less aggressive nation or a smaller nation. I think we are being true hypocrites if we allow that to happen. We cannot allow that to happen.
I do not think we can allow the story to be distorted. I believe to a degree that is happening. We are simply attempting to maintain the peace. I do not pretend to have all the answers to what is going on in the Persian Gulf. I simply do not. There are many experts in this House who go far beyond my abilities in this area, but as a Canadian I probably have more at risk in this matter than virtually everyone in this House. Why is this? It is because my son will be engaged in that conflict. It is something I do not want to see happen. It is as simple as that. I do not.
If we could avoid it, we would do everything in our power to avoid it, but it is something that we cannot. It is reality staring me in the face, staring our nation in the face. We cannot avoid it. My wife at this veiy moment is in West Germany to visit our son before he is deployed to the Middle East, to the Persian Gulf. Why? Because, in reality, it could be the last time that my wife and my youngest son will see Greg Junior. It is as simple as that. That is the reality of the tragedy of war. We do not want
Government Orders
it to happen. Hopefully I will be allowed to go over for a couple of days to see my son.
That is the human tragedy of war. There are parents and individuals in this very House whose sons and daughters or grandchildren are over there. Not one of us wants to see it come to the final act of man taking man, human life taking human life. We do not want that to happen.
That is why as a Canadian I can stand here very proudly and look over what we have done as a nation since World War I and certainly since World War II to maintain the peace. I believe in all sincerity that peace is exactly what our Prime Minister wants to achieve, that peace is exactly what our defence minister wants to maintain.
We are not an aggressive nation. We never have been and we never will be. We are a civilized nation that wants to bring about a civilized solution to that mighty problem, but we do not solve a problem by backing away from it. We have the support of almost every civilized nation in the universe, communist nations included or what is left of those communist nations.
That is a strange paradox when we think about it. Could we stand in this House a year ago and say that? No, we could not, but I believe our Secretary of State for External Affairs, our Prime Minister, and our Minister of National Defence have worked very strongly to bring about this sort of unification of spirit in this situation. They have worked very hard. Canada's credibility is certainly on the line. A lot of human emotions are on the line, mine included.
Going back to my opening, none of us want to see the ultimate, which is war. We do not want to see the ultimate inhumanity. Our NDP friends and our Liberal friends do not want to see it. We have taken a position which I believe history will prove right. When we look back a year, two years, five years or ten years from now, I think we could all honourably say that we did the right thing and that we were there for the right reasons: to prevent death, to prevent inhumanity, and to preserve peace.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was moved by what the member said about his own son who

November 28, 1990
Government Orders
will be in the Persian Gulf. I want to say a few words about paying the price.
This afternoon the Canadian parliamentary group, some 40 members of Parliament, met with representatives of Baltic peoples, Canadians of Baltic heritage. We talked about paying the price and freedom being snatched from the Baltic States some 50 years ago. It reminded me, as we were sitting in the West Block discussing something that happened 50 years ago, of how we might be able to right the situation. Here we are in the House tonight talking about freedom having been snatched from the people of Kuwait by the Iraqis, and the price that has to be paid by Canadians who are there, the hostages who are there. We were most pleased today that five of those hostages will be released.
What is happening is not just about that region itself. It is about the goals of our foreign policies that it is built upon. It is the foundation, goals which are peaceful and prosperous, goals which permit Canada to live in freedom. The Baltic people have not been able to live in freedom. Now the people of Kuwait cannot live in freedom. As the member has said, a price has been paid. We cannot let ourselves remain silent. We cannot fool ourselves into believing that we are isolated from events of this magnitude.
I would just like to say to the hon. member that his commitment is strong. His resolute is strong as his own family member is involved in this. I would also like to say that recently the constituents of Scarborough Centre promptly responded to a questionnaire supporting the government's position that Canada should play a role in the Persian Gulf, a role which has been fully consistent with the United Nations to date, including the enforcement of economic sanctions.

Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to take part in this debate. I have sat here throughout the evening listening to many great speakers, and I want to state that I support, in principle, the Canadian government's actions in condemning the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq, by joining late with the United Nations and countries around the world to say that this type of activity cannot be allowed to go unchallenged, and that Canada would do the right thing, as it did, and participate in the naval blockade of Iraq.
From the moment Iraqi tanks rolled into Kuwait in August, there has been world-wide agreement that they must leave. The only question was how to make this happen. Some world leaders wanted immediate military action, regardless of whether the international community supported such a move. They believed that this would punish the Iraqi aggressor and ensure that Saddam Hussein would never again threaten the region.
Fortunately, other world leaders campaigned to stop such a move, recognizing that military action would shatter the international consequences in the United Nations. Other leaders promoted a more credible alternative. Since the objective behind the United States, Canada, and the other countries could be said to be the protection of Saudi Arabia from Iraqi attack, and the allies should not attack at all, but rather, declare the measures to be a success. The economic embargo of Iraq could be maintained as punishment. In time, these people argued, Iraq could sue for peace and abandon this occupied territory.
The third most widely appealing option was to combine UN-mandated economic sanctions with the potential for military action under UN agreement. In this option, every diplomatic effort would be exhausted before resorting to force. This is exactly what is happening now.
The Canadian people, through their elected representatives in Parliament, must be given the opportunity to be kept informed and to offer their opinion on the relevant issues. As I studied this motion, I realized that once again the government is trying to get authorization to branch out on its own and act without consulting Parliament. I specifically refer to the end of the motion which reads "subsequent resolutions". This makes me uneasy, as it leaves so many avenues open. The Liberal amendment would prevent the government from once again taking action without consulting Parliament.
If the House agrees to the Liberal amendment, then, and only then, will I support the motion. Without this amendment, we would be allowing the government to take action on behalf of Canadians without consulting their elected representatives. We would be writing a blank cheque to the government.
If there is one clear message that should come out of this debate tonight and tomorrow, it is this. Canada must be an advocate of patience. It must use its influence on the United Nations Security Council. It must argue for a
November 28, 1990

diplomatic solution. There must be a clear understanding, agreed to by all of us, that sanctions must be given a chance and a peaceful solution should result, certainly not one of war.
Throughout two world wars and the Korean War, Canada was recognized as one of the greatest fighting nations on the face of this earth. After this, we have become a peacekeeping nation, a reputation earned to a great degree, by the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson. Lately, Canada has always filled the role as peacekeeper. That is exactly how we want to continue to be known. A peaceful solution must come of this.
I am in no way trying to minimize the fact that the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq must not be tolerated and that there is support for Canadian action to date in participating in the international effort to make sanctions work. We must all keep in mind that if war breaks out, there is no way of telling how many casualties there will be and how many of our men and women will lose their lives.
We all agree, I believe, that Saddam Hussein is a madman. He is a man who must be stopped. Maybe the only way to stop him will be by force. However, if this is true, this must be debated fully in this Parliament. This is why I stand here tonight and say that, if we are to support this motion, it must be amended so that any resolution undertaken by the Security Council tomorrow must be debated in the House of Commons before Canada participates.
Christmas is fast approaching and this House will be recessing. But, if we must debate it, whether it be on December 25, December 31, or on January 1, we must debate it before further Canadian action would be taken.
Saddam Hussein is a serious threat to international peace, and the Charter of the United Nations which forbids acts of aggression must be supported. The security of other states in the region must be secured. I cannot stress enough how important it is that we settle this crisis with peace rather than with war.
On Tuesday last, the Leader of the Opposition questioned the Prime Minister stating that:
Speaking to an American Senate committee this morning, former
American Defence Secretary James Schlesinger said that so far,
Government Orders
economic sanctions against Iraq have produced the expected results,
but might have to be maintained for a whole year if they are to have
a decisive impact. His opinion is shared by a good many
international affairs experts.
The Leader asked the Prime Minister if he shares the views of these experts and, if not, why not.
In response, the Prime Minister did not bother to provide full information on the effectiveness of the sanctions. This can only lead one to believe that perhaps the Prime Minister is reluctant to let us in on the facts about sanctions, because there is evidence that they are working.
Since the Second World War, no country has been disciplined so strongly and so completely because of its aggression. With such tight sanctions, it is difficult to imagine how Iraq could possibly be better off for having invaded Kuwait. Therefore, I feel that the sanctions should be given a longer period of time, perhaps six months, or perhaps a year. The precise length of time of the sanctions I am not here to debate tonight.
What I am prepared to say is that if sanctions do not achieve their objective, which is the complete withdrawal from Kuwait of Iraqi forces and the assurance that Saddam Hussein does not plan further aggression against neighbouring states, then war will be an option. It cannot be ruled out. If it should become the most viable option for the fulfilment of international objectives, then Canada will support military action at that time.
In any scenario, the government must not be able to take such steps as it did this summer without consulting the people of Canada through Parliament. Therefore, unless this amendment is adopted, I cannot support the government's action.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, have listened carefully today to my colleagues on all sides of the House. I have to say that I think all Canadians have the idea that peace is the most important thing for any country to live by. However, I do feel that there are a few elements in this debate that have been whitewashed and perhaps have to be reviewed.
My colleague mentioned the use of sanctions and the length of time, and I agree totally with everything that has been said. I agree with the last speaker for the government as to the need to find peace.

November 28, 1990
Government Orders
I think Canadians should realize that the importance of this debate tonight has been to show Canadians that once again we have a government that is proceeding faster than we should be proceeding.
One of the saddest things I have heard was one of our three members who are in Iraq on the radio tonight saying that our government, our country had not done enough to free the hostages over there. I think this is what we have forgotten in this process today.
We have not asked ourselves if we have done enough, before asking for a resolution based on something that may pass in the future, or tomorrow, at the United Nations?
I will deal with that because I asked the Minister of Defence a question specifically about it. I do not think we have tried hard enough as a country who has had a role for peacekeeping that has been well accepted throughout the world to help the remaining hostages in Iraq and Kuwait. We have not tried either in the sense of using the United Nations properly. We have resolutions of the United Nations and we have all the economic sanctions, including the sea and air transport in and out of Iraq. We have not given them time to be effective, in my view.
Furthermore, we have no reporting mechanism to anyone about the effect of the economic sanctions. We just have to accept the information coming from one source or another. There is no UN statement coming out as to the effect. I know that the chairmanship of the United Nations today is in the hands of the United States and that that chairmanship changes to another country at the end of this month. I also know that a chairman of any committee controls the work program of that committee.
I do not want to get into the reasons why we are perhaps on the verge of exercising more force in the Persian Gulf. There will be another day to argue whether they are valid reasons for Canadians, or whether it is business interests like some have implied here tonight.
It may be big business interests in the Middle East that are forcing us into this. We did not go to war or even take this type of precaution in the crisis with Lebanon or in Central America. The draft resolution that is before the UN this week would change the mandate of our forces when they went over initially, which was to enforce
economic sanctions. It was not to try and restore peace, as it says in the draft resolution.
We are asked here tonight by this government to pass a motion that supposes something in the future. Our amendment says that we do not mind passing a motion supporting all that the UN has done until today, but not a motion in the House that may or may not have a future resolution. Economic sanctions may start to work tomorrow. Why are we prejudging what the Security Council may or may not do tomorrow by passing a resolution in this House, by pre-empting a process that I think all of us have had a lot of respect for, and that is the United Nations. I do not think there has been any effort on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs or our officials at the UN to try and find what the reporting mechanism is going to be for the member states who are taking part in forcing the economic sanctions in the gulf. There is no mechanism. Furthermore, there is no mechanism within the draft resolution tomorrow that would have a reporting of the necessary force or the necessary means to keep peace in the Persian Gulf.
It is committee 661, that Canada co-chaired.
Resolution 661, you mean.
The committee that created that resolution.

You are talking about the military committee and I have not heard them report anywhere. I have not seen them report once. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary will produce the reports of the committee.
However, I can say that we are rushing into an element that has all the hardships of losing a very secure role that we have played up until now, and the role that we have played up until tonight in the gulf. We are being asked to change that and are being asked by this government to pass a motion that will sanction its future moves, probably without having to come back to Parliament. If we sanction the motion tonight or tomorrow, and it will not be because the opposition is voting with it, we are sanctioning future resolutions. It gives the appearance that Parliament has debated and passed something that we have not had an opportunity to debate.
November 28, 1990

The vagueness of the government's motion, in its efforts to assure compliance with the Security Council resolution 660 and subsequent resolutions-and the offensive part is "subsequent resolutions", because it is vague as to what is subsequent resolutions-would be clearly defined if today's date was put in. In the future, we could come back to this House and debate any future resolutions that may be passed by the United Nations. But no, this government wants to pre-empt the Security Council and give the government cane blanche to change the role in the Persian Gulf without coming back to Parliament if the United Nations goes ahead.
In the summer, we saw troops leave Halifax without a resolution as to why they were going to the Persian Gulf. It was not until they were in Gibraltar, I think, that they got the-

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to join in this debate this evening. I particularly congratulate the government for bringing this debate forward in response, I might say, to requests put forward by various members of the opposition in the last few days and, indeed, because it is the proper thing to do.
It is appropriate that the Parliament of Canada should come together and discuss events as serious as those which have taken place in the Persian Gulf and the implication of the possibility that, for the first time in 37 years, Canadians have been drawn into hostile action.
But the debate we are engaged in today is not about war, it is about peace. The actions of the United Nations are about peace and about how best to bring forward peace. If we want to talk about war, quite frankly, war began on August 2 for the people of Kuwait and, by implication, war began on August 2 for the people of the world, the people who believe that the arbitrary actions of a medieval dictator like Saddam Hussein should not be tolerated in the world.
The events we have seen in the last year or so have been extraordinary and we thought the world was coming together for the first time. Now we are faced with this situation that brings us back down to earth and reminds us that, no matter how civilized the peoples of the world become, there will always be those who cannot play by
Government Orders
the rules of civilized people. That is what the debate is about today.
What we have seen take place in the last three months is an extraordinary coming together of the peoples of the world, united through the vehicle of the United Nations, an institution whose credibility, quite frankly in recent years has been brought into question. What we have seen in the last three months is the renewal of the credibility of the United Nations.
I welcome the debate that is taking place this evening. There is something I regret, other than what has gone on with Mr. Saddam Hussein and his supporters who have made necessary the actions of the nations that have come together at the United Nations and, indeed, have made necessary this debate in Parliament today.
There is a second thing that I regret. I must say that honestly I regret the message might go out across the world, to Canadian forces in the gulf, that Canadians do not stand united on this issue, that Canadians do not speak with one voice on this issue, and that is something regrettable.
I do not know and I certainly do not wish to attribute motivation to my hon. friends opposite with respect to what is going on here in this discussion and, indeed, this debate tonight.

I read the amendments of the hon. members opposite, both from the Liberal Party and the NDP. Those amendments are saying that Canada tomorrow is not prepared to stand with the United Nations. That is what they are saying. They are saying: "Let's wait. Let's debate. Let's not take a strong stand. Let's not tell this man that the world is not prepared to tolerate his actions". That is what they are saying on the other side. They are proposing that we show exactly what the leader of Iraq is looking to see from the western world. He is looking to see the cracks. He is looking to see those who would break ranks. He is looking to see the weakness and that is precisely what we must not show him.
I cannot help but wonder what would have been said in this country. Canadians are not used to war. It has been 37 years since our troops faced hostile action. What would have been said in 1950? What would Prime Minister St. Laurent have said about the opposition in Parliament that day when the United Nations said: "We have to stand together". If the Parliament of Canada had

November 28, 1990
Government Orders
had to debate, if the people on the other side had said at that time: "We will not stand with the government because whatever this government does we are against". What would the Right Hon. Mackenzie King have said in 1939 if the opposition of the day had stood against the government of that time? I cannot help but think to myself that Neville Chamberlain would have been very much at home in the Liberal Party of Canada today. And what message is being sent out by that action?
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, there are two messages that the Parliament of this country must send out. One message should be sent to Mr. Saddam Hussein and that is that Canada stands with the world, that Canada is not prepared to tolerate countries invading its neighbours.
I listened earlier to my hon. friends from the NDP saying: "We must give sanctions time to work". Sanctions have not worked for 30 years in South Africa, but we must wait and let sanctions work. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, I do not care what the NDP thinks, sanctions are not good enough for the people of Kuwait.
I heard talk about children being killed in the war. Nobody wants to see children killed, nobody wants to see men or women killed. But tell it to the people of Kuwait. That is who the NDP should be talking to.
The message that we must send first and foremost is that Canada stands with the world.
Second, we must send a message to our troops, to our men and women who are in the gulf. Seventy per cent of those people live in Nova Scotia, my province. I know some of the people who are over there, former friends and colleagues in the navy. We must send a message to them that Canada stands united behind them, that Canada appreciates the courage that they are showing by being there.
We heard earlier a very eloquent speech from an hon. colleague from Carleton-Charlotte. He talked about his personal involvement with his son being over there. Mr. Speaker, that is certainly a very difficult act to follow. I do appreciate the member's words and I do concur with him 100 per cent.
I would like to express my support tonight for the resolution we are discussing and point out some of Canada's responsibilities in this particular crisis. We have a long history as peacekeepers and we do have the
November 28, 1990

responsibility today to help restore the peace in the Persian Gulf.
As a member of the United Nations Security Council, we have the responsibility to uphold the charter of the United Nations and all of its resolutions. Ultimately, as the Government of Canada, we have the responsibility to explain to Canadians the role we intend to play in this particular crisis.
The background of this whole situation is well known to all of us. We are aware of the details of how on August 2 Iraq invaded Kuwait. This unprovoked, brutal and most monstrous act of aggression shocked the whole world and triggered one of the most serious international crises of recent times. It was a flagrant violation of international law and has been condemned by the whole international community. Despite the United Nations resolutions creating an international trade embargo and sanctions, Mr. Hussein has seen not fit to back down. Many foreigners, including 45 Canadians, are still being held hostage in Iraq. The threat of future violence toward Saudi Arabia and any other of the gulf states is still a real possibility.
While the sanctions have perhaps produced some changes in the position of Iraq, the Americans and others tell us that it will be perhaps a year before they take effect. I think we need to recognize what the delay while waiting for the sanctions to take a full effect would have. I believe that as we consider the build-up and development of nuclear arms by Iraq and stockpiling of chemical weapons, we realize the threat to all of the peaceful countries in the Middle East.
Mr. Hussein has been described as crazy, but I do not believe he is. I believe he is very shrewd and calculating, and as we have already seen, a very unpredictable person. His recent attempts to lead the whole Arab world against Israel are a very dangerous ploy and will lead to further destabilization in the Middle East.
The motion before us this evening is to support the United Nations resolution which demands that Iraq comply fully with resolution 660 and all subsequent resolutions. This resolution provides Iraq with one final opportunity to remove all of its troops from Kuwait and release the foreign hostages. If this is not done, the resolution authorizes member states to use all necessary
Government Orders
means to bring an end to this crises. While this does not necessarily mean the immediate use of troops, it does allow those in charge of the UN forces to use force it necessary.
In supporting this motion, we would be supporting the use of force which many feel would be inconsistent with our responsibilities to our traditional peacekeeping role.
We have to ask ourselves this evening what it really means to be peacekeepers. I believe that peacekeeping is an integral part of not only preserving the peace, but sometimes restoring it when it has been disturbed, such as has happened in the Middle East.
As Canadians, we can be justifiably proud of our role as peacekeepers. In March of this year we had the privilege to visit Cyprus where we visited the Canadian troops, who have an excellent role and an excellent reputation as peacekeepers.
We are familiar with the role that Canadians played in the Suez crisis in the 1950s. It was our country under the then Secretary of State for External Affairs, Lester Pearson, who pioneered the United Nations Emergehcy Force, for which he won the Nobel Peace Prize.
Canada is the only member of the United Nations to have participated in all of the major peacekeeping operations. Our record spans four decades and include operations both within and without the UN auspices. Considering this history, we cannot abandon our role and responsibility as peacekeepers.
A very significant statement was made by our Prime Minister when he said: "Our traditional peacekeeping role neither excludes nor excuses us from the call to resist aggression".
The United Nations Charter does not provide a definition of peacekeeping either. However, peacekeeping reflects one of the first purposes of the UN announced in its preamble to the Charter when it says: "The establishment of conditions under which justice and respect for obligations arising from treaties and other sources of international law can be maintained".
Peacekeeping goes hand in hand with peacemaking. To quote the Secretary General: "As regards international peace and security, the United Nations Charter sets out a process which in its first stage is based on the

November 28, 1990
Government Orders
renunciation of force in international relations and on the peaceful settlement of disputes".
If these principles are rejected, the Charter provides for a collective enforcement by the world community through the Security Council. Such actions range from various forms of embargoes to the use of military forces by the Security Council.
While I believe that we must use every diplomatic tool that we have, one of the best diplomacy tools that we have is to back up our diplomacy with a legitimate threat of force. If approved, the United Nations resolution will strengthen our diplomatic message and convey to Mr. Hussein that disregard for international law cannot, nor will not, be tolerated. Iraq must understand the conviction and the determination of the international community.
A second responsibility we must uphold is our responsibility as a member of the Security Council of the United Nations. As a member of the Security Council, we are responsible for maintaining international peace and security in accordance with the purposes and principles of the UN.
In the event of a threat to peace or an act of aggression, we are to make recommendations as to what action should be taken. We are doing that in this case.
This can include, under the provisions of the Charter, chapter 7, the enforcement action by UN member states, including the use of armed forces or other collective measures for dealing with threats to the peace, breaches of the peace, or acts of aggression.
Canada has played an integral role in the creation of the United Nations and has been actively involved since the beginning. When we were elected to the Security Council two years ago, we won on the first ballot with 80 per cent of the member states voting for us.
We should be very proud as a country to be held in such high esteem throughout the world. How can we let those countries down that voted us to the Security Council when we are faced with such a difficult situation?
When Canada was first elected, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the seriousness of our commitment, said that our role would be to react to issues as they arise, depending on the issue, its timing, its connection to other issues and the crucial question of what is finally possible. He said the question of what is finally possible
does not, unfortunately, always conform to what is desirable.
To quote from the speech of our Secretary of State for External Affairs to the United Nations Association, he said: "We will face the choice of working and voting for imperfect compromises that have some chance of success as opposed to speaking and voting for resolutions that sound great, but cannot be applied. This government has no illusions that some of our positions in the Security Council will from time to time displease segments of the Canadian public". This is one of those times. We agree that not everybody is going to agree with what we are doing. However, this is no excuse to shrink from our responsibility to the world community.
Some have accused the government of saying: "How high?" to the United States command of "Jump". This is an insult, as was mentioned earlier tonight, not only to Canada, but to France, the United Kingdom and many other countries that are involved in the Middle East. As the nation with the greatest resources, I believe it is natural that the United States should be the leader in this particular engagement.
This brings me to the last and final responsibility, and that is our responsibility as a government to keep Canadians informed of our position and the role we intend to play. I am glad that we have had this debate tonight to present Canada's position on the proposed UN resolution. I encourage the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister to continue to allow Parliament to play an important part in these decisions.
I support the motion and I hope that our decisions are made in Canada for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the hour grows late, and I mean much more than the hour on the clock across from me. Just a year ago the world rejoiced as the walls came tumbling down and peace and democracy seemed to be sweeping huge parts of the world, where for decades the suppression of human potential and human freedom had been the norm. The cold war was ending and for the first time in 50 years we were seeing the possibility of turning the world's resources from instruments of death and destruction to feeding the hungry of the world, nurturing her children and reversing the devastating damage we do
November 28, 1990

every day to the bounty of the earth and to the very ability of our planet to sustain life.
Now we find ourselves on the brink of war. We find Canada turning its back on the role for which we have become one of the most respected nations of the world, the role of peacemaker and peacekeeper. That role, despite what we have heard from the government side tonight, has not been a role of wimpish submission to aggression or to the violation of human rights. It has been one of going courageously into dangerous situations, acting with restraint but with the clear objective that our forces were there to prevent the outbreak of hostilities, of violence, of killing and that our diplomatic efforts in other places were sustaining and supporting their efforts to prevent war.
Now instead we have adopted a warmongering, sabre-rattling stance. We hear our Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and the Minister of National Defence saying: "We will do what needs to be done with or without the United Nations".
It is important to understand what is before us tonight. The only purpose of the motion before us is to supersede a motion that was adopted by this House just a month ago, a motion that says we abhor the aggression against Kuwait, we support the United Nations resolutions calling for sanctions and we commit the Government of Canada reporting back to the Canadian people through their elected Parliament if further action is to be taken in the Middle East.
The government now wants to supersede that. It wants a wide open door to take whatever action it deems appropriate, without the responsibility to report to Parliament and to account to Canadians for its actions.
It is also important to understand what the motion is that will be dealt with by the Security Council tomorrow and that the government wants to support on behalf of the people of Canada. For a week now we have been subjected to suggestions and statements about what this motion is. I question whether many members on the other side have read the motion.
We have heard that this is a necessary step so that the United Nations can act with force. That is not what the motion says. The motion authorizes member states, not
Government Orders
the United Nations, but any one of those member states, to take all necessary means to uphold and implement Security Council resolution 660 and subsequent resolutions, that is to have Iraq withdraw from Kuwait. Any one of those member states, with whatever weapons are at their disposal, with or without the rest of the United Nations members, is authorized by this motion to act.
Furthermore, those same member states are authorized to use all necessary means to restore international peace and security in the area. That goes far beyond Kuwait and Iraq. That can touch any one of a number of volatile situations in the Middle East. I ask the members opposite to think of all the countries in the United Nations, many of which are countries in the Middle East, and ask whether we really want, as a country, to give UN sanction to any one of those states in taking the action they think is necessary to "restore international peace and security in this area".
We are all aware of the numerous difficult and volatile situations that exist in that part of the world. Why does the Prime Minister want this carte blanche, not for the United Nations, but for the member states of the United Nations? What justification has he provided this House? Just as the government refused to come before Parliament and justify why we were putting Canadian men and women into a potential war zone in the first place, he has now refused to tell us what sanctions have accomplished, what they could accomplish by Christmas Day, what they could accomplish by January 15, and how long we would need sanctions to work. Frankly, how he can ask us on the basis of no justification as to what is happening with the sanctions to get this kind of open door to any further action without the specific information coming before this Parliament, I do not understand.
The Prime Minister says "trust me" but what reason have we to trust. He wraps himself in the United Nations flag, but it was not on the basis of the UN resolution that we committed troops to the Persian Gulf. We did that two weeks before the United Nations passed any resolution. It was not on the basis of any United Nations resolution that we moved our troops from outside the gulf to inside the gulf. It was not on the basis of any United Nations resolution, it was on the basis of a statement by the U.S. air force chief of staff that the

November 28, 1990
Government Orders
U.S. was prepared to unleash a massive bombing attack against Baghdad that we committed our CF-18s.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said this motion is not a threat. Of course it is a threat. I question whether those who are making those threats, rattling those sabres, even understand the enemy well enough to know what effect this threat will have. We have assumed an air of superiority that discounts the values that guide the Arab nations and guide Iraq. We are not prepared to deal with them because we do not give them any credibility.
Horrible crimes have been committed against our own humanity when we fail to give value to each and every life on this planet. Hitler was able to perpetrate the Holocaust based on the belief that Jews were not quite human. Atrocities happened in Vietnam based on the views that people with yellow skin and slanted eyes were not quite human. Violence against women and children continues because we are able to convince ourselves that they are not quite human.
The UN was formed with the determination to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war. Surely we have progressed in our evolution as human beings beyond where we believe that only brute force is the way to resolve disputes. We should make no mistake in this volatile situation that a war puts at risk nothing less than the survival of the world.
I do not believe for one moment in appeasement or acquiescence or acceding to the aggression of a Saddam Hussein. Killing is not the only way to be tough. Sometimes it takes more toughness, more courage and more strength to last out a peaceful resolution of aggression.
I would like to see Canada taking much more of a leadership role in this issue than we have done. We look to the United Nations and welcome its concerted action, yet every day we continue to biologically and chemically destroy our world. The Minister of the Environment tells us that he won't take any action on that destruction of our world until two years from now when we might have an international agreement.
The appalling contradiction in our words and actions is diminishing Canada's reputation internationally and I call upon the government to either accept the amendment to this motion or to withdraw it and to let stand the motion of October 19 that we support the UN in sanctions; we will continue those sanctions until the aggression is undone and we will do nothing further until we come back to this Parliament and speak to the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, we cannot and will not vote for this motion because it leaves far too many questions unanswered. The motion asks our Parliament to endorse not just one, but many Security Council resolutions, as spelled out in the motion before us, including resolutions whose wording we do not know because they have not been finalized nor passed. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State to External Affairs, in his intervention, revealed the weakness of this aspect of the resolution some five hours ago.
Second, we will not support it because the effect of sanctions which we all subscribe to and support is still unknown and has just begun to be felt.
Third, we will not support it because the environmental consequences both in human and ecological terms are frightening.
I would like to put on record in that respect a few paragraphs from a speech given by the King of Jordan, His Majesty King Hussein I, some three weeks ago in Geneva on the occasion of the Second World Conference on Climate Warming. He said:
A war in the Gulf would not only result in devastating human death and injury, tremendous economic loss, and prolonged political confrontation between Orient and Occident. It could also lead to an environmental catastrophe the likes of which the world has not experienced since the accident at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant-A war in the Gulf could result in the use of chemical and biological weapons, and widespread destruction to oil fields and oil storage depots.
The preliminary calculations of our scientists indicate that if half Kuwait's oil reserves (or about 50 billion barrels) were to go up in flames during a war, the environmental impact would be swift, severe and devastating. Emissions of carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide would surpass internationally accepted safety standards by factors of hundreds, and, without factoring in wind effects, would blacken the skies over a radius of at least 750 kilometres from Kuwait-that is, all of Kuwait, Iraq, Bahrain, Qatar, the Emirates and the waters of the Gulf, and most of Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Syria and Iran.
Other than poisonous emissions of carbon monoxide and sulphur dioxide, the emission of carbon dioxide will increase by at least a factor of 100 over the current total global emission of 5.5 billion tons a year. Lingering in the atmosphere for around 100 years, this massive C02 emission would promote the greenhouse effect, and contribute to
November 28, 1990

global warming, climatic changes, lower global food production, and human and animal health deterioration.
The environmental and human toll of such a scenario would be beyond our wildest fears. If oil production facilities suffered longterm damage, which is likely in the event of war, the catastrophe we warn of would be compounded by the devastating impact of the loss of oil imports for economies and peoples around the world.
Because of time limitations I will not go beyond these major quotations from that speech.
It seems to me that the premise that we ought to adopt as a civilized society with the record that Canada has would be that it is in the Persian Gulf an illusion to believe that peace can be attained through an act of war.
I am referring, in particular, to an editorial in The Globe and Mail today which is pursuing this perverse logic, trying to convince its readership that we can pursue peace through an act of war in the Persian Gulf.
Second, the United Nations is an instrument of peace. It should not be involved in offensive actions.
Third, Canada should pursue a policy of voting against any possible offensive action in the gulf, not subscribe to potential ones and ask the Parliament of Canada to subscribe to commit itself to subsequent resolutions, the wording of which we do not know. The draft which is in our possession and to which colleagues of mine have made reference earlier was produced on Monday of this week and has already been put on record on several occasions. It would give a green light and a blank cheque to the use of all necessary means to uphold and implement Security Council resolution 660 and all subsequent relevant resolutions.
I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs would not, in all honesty, expect Parliament to submit itself to resolutions that have not yet been drafted, agreed upon, and passed by virtue of this draft that is in our possession as of Monday of this week from the Canadian mission in New York.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly not.

I am glad to hear that the parliamentary secretary concurs with that.
Government Orders
It seems to us that major features of Canadian policies have to be formulated as they have been by the distinguished Leader of the Senate group in the other place, who said on November 20 that Canada's policy should consist of major features:
First, Canada should work principally through the United Nations and not bilaterally-
Second, while safeguarding humanitarian action, medical supplies and food supplies, Canada should favour putting the maximum amount of pressure on Iraq to withdraw from Kuwait, short of offensive aciion.
Third, an early report should be obtained -
We have complained about all afternoon and evening:
- from the Security Council sanctions committee to be made public and discussed in the Canadian Parliament.
Fourth, Canada should make it clear that it will not consider offensive military action in the Gulf-
Fifth, Canadian land forces should not be sent to the Gulf area -
Sixth, Canada should initiate rounds of consultation with the countries concerned to find ways of de-escalating the conflict.
Finally, the Canadian government should not initiate or participate in offensive action without bringing the issue before both Houses of Parliament.
What we are witnessing, instead, is an erratic course of action of this government, not a well thought out policy that is implemented according to some very clearly set premises and principles.
There is agreement in this House it seems to me at the end of this debate on two points. First, we all agree that the action on the part of Iraq invading in Kuwait ought to be rejected, has been rejected, and must continue to be rejected and condemned. Second, there is no one in the House who would disagree that we fully support the use of sanctions. But beyond that we part ways.
We as Liberals are convinced that the solution to the Persian Gulf crisis must be found through dialogue and negotiations, not through armed conflict. The UN's role in this issue will not be ultimately successful and the world body prestige enhanced if it is not actively involved in the peace process.
Why is Canada not discussing ideas for a peacekeeping force, for instance? It has not been pursued in the Security Council by Canada, consistent with the tradition and experience that we have in this respect. How about

Government Orders
the UN led strategy for curbing the global arms threat to avoid a repetition of the situation?
We believe that Canadians are looking for answers to creative questions and not to initiatives that we are being asked to pursue by way of commitments which would inevitably lead to Canada being involved in aggressive initiatives in the gulf area.
In his intervention this afternoon the Secretary of State for External Affairs failed to prove his case. It was his responsibility to convince this House that there was urgency and an absolute necessity for Parliament to endorse this resolution. Instead he engaged in an elaboration of an historical nature as to what has happened so far and urged Parliament to follow the lead without, however, giving us the reasons for doing so.
Mr. Speaker, I see you signalling. I appreciate the opportunity for this intervention at this late hour.

However if we agree, by unanimous consent, to limit it just to those on your list, the debate does come to an early conclusion and in fact rewards the patience of those of us who have sat here and waited so long to speak, because it was one of the most important issues we can face, an issue of life and death.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to be here to participate in this debate, even though the hour is late. As the previous interchange has indicated that my time will be quite
November 28, 1990

limited, I would like to deal with some of the highlights of what I had planned to say.
We have heard many words of high principle and abstract thoughts about the nature of the United Nations, the international community, international law, and so on.
We are also talking about a very stark reality, a reality that is very clear, for example, to the 18-year-old in the Co-op service station that I went into on the weekend. He asked whether, in fact, he would be subject to a draft as a foreseeable consequence of the actions of the government and the United Nations in the Middle East, something that he felt personally to be a fear for him.
The fears that this young man expressed are indicative of the thoughts going through the minds of many young people in the country. We too often ignore that it is those people facing the direct reality, and not those of us who sit in the House.
At the other end, there are people probably not many blocks from here, and people in the Pentagon who are perhaps at this very moment, if they work this late, planning meticulously what would happen under various scenarios. How many people would die, how they would die, and when they would die. These things are well planned in advance and, if the people of Canada had that kind of information laid before them by the government, rather than lofty rhetoric and appeals to emotion, it might well cast a much different light on the question we are debating. That is the reality of what we are talking about tonight.
I certainly stand with my party and, in fact, the whole opposition in opposing the resolution put forward by the government. I do so for several reasons and many of those have been expressed veiy well by other speakers tonight. Basically, we cannot issue a blank cheque for what will happen after January 15. With all due respect, I do not think we can issue our own government a blank cheque for what will happen after January 15. I do not think, given the wording of the UN resolution which allows any member of the international community to take action, we cannot allow a blank cheque there either. It has been clear as these things evolved through the
Government Orders
summer-the Oka dispute and our first excursion into the gulf-that, in fact, the government is prepared to move well ahead of the authority it has from Parliament and to move well ahead of the rationale which it might be offering.
This whole scenario and the resolution before us indicate that what we might have been doing up to now might well have been a fraud, in that it implies that we never were serious about sanctions, that the UN body was never serious about sanctions, that the U.S. was never serious about sanctions, and that the objective was always to invade and engage in a military conflict. Surely, all our experience with sanctions-and there has been considerable experience with sanctions internationally- has indicated that sanctions would not work this fast. It is silly to say that the possibilities of sanctions have been exhausted or would be exhausted by January 15. That clearly is not within the realm of imagination, especially when we are being asked again to accept a blank cheque when there has been no evidence before us that the sanctions are not working.
This was underlined when we heard the member from Surrey say: "What if it takes a year for sanctions to work?" Well, what if it takes a year for sanctions to work? Surely, a year of sanctions is a much preferable scenario than a blood-bath involving our own young men and women in the Middle East. Spending a year to make sure that sanctions work and engaging in other forms of international pressure are surely preferable to engaging in a blood-bath in the Middle East.
I was disturbed in this debate by the questioning of the motives of people who perhaps do not support this resolution and the implication that perhaps those who oppose the government's resolution, somehow or other, are condoning the actions of Saddam Hussein, are in favour of the expansionism, and of the flouting international law. I would like to ask the government, does it feel that the motives of people like the Christian Peacemaker Teams, a group from the Church of the Brethren, the Brethren in Christ, the Mennonite Church and the General Conference Mennonite Church, the delegation that departed last weekend, should be questioned. I might add that I might well have been a member of that delegation if Federal Express had not sent my passport to Winnipeg instead of Washington.

Government Orders
This delegation has been in Iraq for some days. Their objective was to meet with Iraqi families, to visit non-religious institutions such as hospitals, schools and other projects to communicate concerns for a just peace with the political leaders in Baghdad and so on.
I received a fax today from that delegation. Some of the things they say are interesting. It says: "Shortages are beginning. Sugar, milk, medical supplies, petrol additives, water purification chemicals are all in short supply". It says: "Everyone is growing in apprehension and conviction about the crisis". It says further: "In other meetings senior Iraqis underlined their desire to negotiate and said that they await a 'hint' of interest from the U.S.". All of these are indications to me that the sanctions are working, that the effects are being felt. Surely it is very much premature at this point to say that sanctions are not working.
We also have heard an appeal to principle, the principles of international law. It strikes me as ironic. My first experience at the United Nations came when I was making an intervention on behalf of East Timor at the same time as the initial debates were occurring in the Security Council regarding the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait at the beginning of August. It was an interesting juxtaposition, where on the one hand the world community was solidly condemning the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq, while at the same time totally ignoring the invasion of East Timor by Indonesia 15 years ago. The international community has been silent on that question ever since.
It struck me that it must be a matter of who ends up with the oil. In the case of Iraq obviously the bad guys ended up with the oil and in the case of East Timor the good guys ended up with the oil. That seems to be very much what these high flown principles come down to when they are examined closely.
In conclusion, I would like to urge the government to not let us go down the slippery slope that we are on, to not let ourselves get sucked into a situation that we cannot get out of, to not engage in a kind of demoniza-tion that allows us no options. Canada has been a leader in the search for peace internationally. We are not showing leadership now. Let us show leadership again. As a former cultural hero of a particular generation said:
"Let's give the sanctions a chance, let's give peace a chance".
