Mr. Speaker, I think that is certainly regrettable. It is regrettable that the government has seen fit to do this. We have heard the arguments on why and they can be judged by the public. Mr. Speaker, I think in a few moments we will have finished this. What I would like to do is basically communicate to this House the feeling of my constituents. After all, we all represent a large number of people in this House of Commons, where the issues are aired and they are decided.
The people I represent do support the United Nations and they support it vigorously. They believe that the United Nations and its collective security approach is the only way to go. The allegations that that is not true, that I do not support it, my colleagues do not, and the people I represent do not is false.
November 28, 1990

They do not support Saddam Hussein. They do not support the invasion of Kuwait. They are not weak on this. They are absolutely firm. So am I as are my colleagues.
They do not believe, however, that the Canadian Armed Forces should be used to attack Iraq. The reason they do not believe that is that at the present time there is no one shooting inside Kuwait, or Iraq is not shooting at its neighbours at this point. The situation has stopped.
We believe that this government and the United States in the United Nations will convince their United Nations colleagues to use force to attack when nobody is actually shooting at this point for whatever reason, and we believe that is absolutely wrong. A million people will die, most of them women and children, but certainly members of the Canadian Armed Forces will die, and they could die in large numbers if the conflict takes on the complexion of the Iran-Iraq war. Americans will die in large numbers, as will members of the armed forces of every' other nation. We will kill probably a million Iraqis as well, women and children, the elderly. It will be an absolute blood-bath.
That is what we have before us tonight. My constituents do not believe that that should happen, in spite of the polls that appear, in spite of what the government might believe.
The other thing they do not believe is the Prime Minister of Canada. Part of the dilemma of this country on the unity issue and on so many other issues is that the Prime Minister of Canada has lost the confidence of the nation. He is not viewed as a strong leader in whom the confidence of the citizenry exists.
What they fear the most and what I fear the most is that this open-ended resolution has been constructed by intelligent people to leave room for the government to
Government Orders
act unilaterally. We have heard backbenchers stand in this House, even cabinet ministers, and say: "Oh, no, we would never do anything like that".
They have in fact done that before. I would point to the GATT agreement on the west coast in which the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, now the Minister of Indian Affairs, stood up and said: "We will never let this thing come to pass. It would be catastrophic for the people on the west coast". The Prime Minister said: "Sorry. We are going to let it happen because our friends, the Americans, want that to happen".
We believe that will happen with this situation. When the Americans go, they are going to say to the Prime Minister of this country that he is going with them and that is the reason why we have an open-ended resolution. That is why the United Nations has an open-ended resolution.
The people I represent recognize in this Prime Minister an individual who will leave himself an out to use the Armed Forces, to not call back Parliament and to basically support the Americans who are the primary initiators of this action to leap into a blood-bath in the Middle East. This will be absolutely catastrophic.
I intend to go from this House because I do not believe that the other side of the House is acting in a responsible and honest fashion and I am going to urge citizens in every community to get out to demonstrate and to actively fight this government in its decision to lead us close and into a war in the Persian Gulf.
